# Appendix A: Deriving Causal Strength Under Structure Uncertainty {#sec-appendix-si}

In Bayesian models of causal induction, observed data $D$ can inform both which causal structure generated the data and what parameter values are likely within each structure. This creates two levels of uncertainty. Parameter uncertainty concerns the strengths and base rates associated with a given structure. Structure uncertainty concerns which causal model should be used to interpret those parameters in the first place.

The basic case illustrated in @fig-si contrasts a link structure, $S_1$, with a no-link structure, $S_0$, but the same logic extends to larger hypothesis spaces containing multiple possible causal structures [@griffiths2009theory]. By representing uncertainty over both structures and parameters, the Bayesian approach yields quantities that differ from covariation-based measures such as $\Delta P$ and from the standard Power PC model [@Cheng1997], which estimates causal power under the link structure $S_1$ using maximum likelihood.

## Causal structures and Bayesian learning

In the basic two-structure case, the hypothesis space contains two competing structures that might underlie the relationship between the candidate cause $C$ and the effect $E$ (@fig-si B). Structure $S_0$ represents the hypothesis that there is no causal relation: effect $E$ occurs independently of the candidate cause $C$, generated exclusively by the amalgam of background causes $A$. The competing structure hypothesis $S_1$ states that there is a causal relation, such that effect $E$ is a function of both the background causes $A$ and cause $C$.

Each structure is associated with a set of parameters, denoted as $\theta$. For structure $S_1$, the parameters include the base rate of the target cause $b_c$, the causal strength $w_c$ of $C$ on $E$, and the influence $w_a$ of the background cause $A$. Structure $S_0$ states that there is no causal relationship between $C$ and $E$ and therefore includes only two parameters, the base rate of $C$, $b_c$ and the strength of the background cause $A$, $w_a$. 

A common choice for the prior distributions is independent uniform Beta distributions over each structure’s parameters:

$$
\begin{aligned}
w_a &\sim \operatorname{Beta}(1,1),\\
b_c &\sim \operatorname{Beta}(1,1),\\
w_c &\sim \operatorname{Beta}(1,1) \qquad \text{under } S_1.
\end{aligned}
$$

These flat priors represent an absence of specific prior assumptions about the parameter values, but the framework also allows alternative parameter priors [@Lu2008bayesianpriors; @yeung2015identifying]. Appendix @sec-appendix-ss describes the sparse-and-strong priors used for the conditional strength model.

Using Bayes’ theorem, the posterior probability distribution of each structure’s parameters conditional on the observed data is given by

$$
P(\theta\mid D;S_i)
=
\frac{
P(D\mid\theta;S_i)\,
P(\theta\mid S_i)
}{
P(D\mid S_i)
}.
$$ {#eq-posterior-theta}

where $P(D\mid\theta;S_i)$ is the likelihood of the data given the parameter values, $P(\theta\mid S_i)$ is the prior distribution over parameters, and $P(D\mid S_i)$ is the marginal likelihood of the data under structure $S_i$.

## Likelihood Computation

The likelihood function specifies how probable the observed data are for a given set of parameter values under a particular causal structure. Under the link structure $S_1$, the effect $E$ depends on both the candidate cause $C$ and the background cause $A$. For generative relations, we assume a noisy-OR parameterization [@pearl1988probabilistic; @Cheng1997]. When the candidate cause is present, the candidate cause and the background cause provide independent opportunities to generate the effect:

$$
P(e\mid c;\theta,S_1,\mathrm{gen})
=
w_c+w_a-w_cw_a.
$$ {#eq-noisy-or}

Under this parameterization, $w_c$ represents the probability that the candidate cause generates an effect that would otherwise be absent.

When the candidate cause is absent, the probability of the effect is determined solely by the background cause:

$$
P(e \mid \neg c; \theta,S_1) = w_a.
$$ {#eq-background-effect}

For preventive relations, we use the corresponding noisy-AND-NOT parameterization [@yuille2007noisy; @Griffiths2005]. When the candidate cause is present,

$$
P(e \mid c;\theta,S_1,\mathrm{prev})
=
w_a(1-w_c).
$$ {#eq-noisy-and-not}

Here, $w_c$ represents the probability that the candidate cause prevents an effect that would otherwise be generated by the background cause. In the absence of the candidate cause, the effect probability is again solely determined by the background cause. 

<!-- Under both parameterizations, causal power corresponds to the maximum-likelihood estimate of the candidate cause’s strength $w_c$ under the assumed link structure and functional form [@Cheng1997; @Griffiths2005]. -->

Under the no-link structure $S_0$, the effect is independent of the candidate cause and is generated solely by the background cause. Thus, $w_c$ is fixed to zero and

$$
P(e\mid c;\theta,S_0)
=
P(e\mid \neg c; \theta,S_0)
=
w_a .
$$ {#eq-no-link-effect}

Accordingly, the likelihood of the observed data under $S_0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(D\mid\theta;S_0)
={}&
\left[(1-b_c)(1-w_a)\right]^{N(\neg c,\neg e)}
\\
&\times
\left[(1-b_c)w_a\right]^{N(\neg c,e)}
\\
&\times
\left[b_c(1-w_a)\right]^{N(c,\neg e)}
\\
&\times
\left[b_cw_a\right]^{N(c,e)} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-likelihood-func-S0}

For a noisy-OR (generative) link structure $S_1$, the likelihood is

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(D\mid\theta;S_1)
={}&
\left[(1-b_c)(1-w_a)\right]^{N(\neg c,\neg e)}
\\
&\times
\left[(1-b_c)w_a\right]^{N(\neg c,e)}
\\
&\times
\left[b_c(1-w_c)(1-w_a)\right]^{N(c,\neg e)}
\\
&\times
\left[b_c(w_c+w_a-w_cw_a)\right]^{N(c,e)} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-likelihood-func-S1-gen}

For a noisy-AND-NOT (preventive) link structure, the first two terms remain unchanged because the effect probability in the absence of the candidate cause is still $w_a$. The last two terms are obtained by replacing $P(e\mid c;\theta,S_1)$ with $w_a(1-w_c)$ (@eq-noisy-and-not):

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(D\mid\theta;S_1)
={}&
\left[(1-b_c)(1-w_a)\right]^{N(\neg c,\neg e)}
\\
&\times
\left[(1-b_c)w_a\right]^{N(\neg c,e)}
\\
&\times
\left[b_c(1-w_a(1-w_c))\right]^{N(c,\neg e)}
\\
&\times
\left[b_cw_a(1-w_c)\right]^{N(c,e)} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-likelihood-func-S1-prev}

@eq-likelihood-func-S0, @eq-likelihood-func-S1-gen, and @eq-likelihood-func-S1-prev specify the probability of the observed cell frequencies for fixed parameter values under the no-link, generative-link, and preventive-link structures, respectively. Bayesian inference additionally requires integrating each likelihood over the corresponding prior distribution of its parameters.

## Marginal likelihoods and causal support

The likelihoods in @eq-likelihood-func-S0, @eq-likelihood-func-S1-gen, and @eq-likelihood-func-S1-prev are conditional on fixed parameter values. Bayesian inference over structures instead requires the marginal likelihood of the data under each structure, obtained by averaging the likelihood over that structure’s prior distribution:

$$
P(D\mid S_i)
=
\int P(D\mid \theta;S_i)\,
P(\theta\mid S_i)\,
d\theta .
$$ {#eq-marginal-likelihood}

The marginal likelihood therefore represents how well structure $S_i$ predicts the observed data after accounting for uncertainty about its parameters. For structure $S_1$, the marginal likelihood is given by 

$$
P(D\mid S_1)
=
\iiint
P(D\mid b_c,w_a,w_c;S_1)\,
P(b_c,w_a,w_c\mid S_1)\,
db_c\,dw_a\,dw_c,
$$

whereas for structure $S_0$ it is given by

$$
P(D\mid S_0)
=
\iint
P(D\mid b_c,w_a;S_0)\,
P(b_c,w_a\mid S_0)\,
db_c\,dw_a.
$$

These marginal likelihoods enter both the posterior distribution over parameters within each structure and the posterior probabilities assigned to the competing structures. The relative evidence provided by the data for the link structure over the no-link structure can be summarized by the Bayes factor, $\mathrm{BF}_{10}=P(D\mid S_1)/P(D\mid S_0)$. @Griffiths2005 defined _causal support_ as the logarithm of this ratio, $\log \mathrm{BF}_{10}$, which quantifies how strongly the observed data favor the presence of a causal link.

## Structure posteriors and posterior link probability

The marginal likelihoods provide the basis for updating beliefs about the competing causal structures. Following @griffiths2009theory, we use the posterior probability of the link structure, $P(S_1\mid D)$, as the measure of structural evidence that a causal relation exists.

The posterior probability of each structure, $P(S_1\mid D)$ and $P(S_0\mid D)$, is computed by multiplying each structure’s marginal likelihood by its prior probability and then normalizing across structures:

$$
P(S_i\mid D)
=
\frac{
P(D\mid S_i)P(S_i)
}{
P(D)
},
$$ {#eq-posterior-structures}

with

$$
P(D)
=
\sum_{i\in\{0,1\}} P(D\mid S_i)P(S_i)
=
P(D\mid S_0)P(S_0)
+
P(D\mid S_1)P(S_1).
$$

Thus, in the two-structure case, the posterior link probability corresponds to the posterior probability of link structure $S_1$:

$$
P(S_1\mid D)
=
\frac{
P(D\mid S_1)P(S_1)
}{
P(D\mid S_1)P(S_1)
+
P(D\mid S_0)P(S_0)
}.
$$

This quantity expresses the posterior probability that the observed data were generated by a structure containing a causal link from $C$ to $E$, rather than by the no-link structure. Unless denoted otherwise, we use uniform priors over the two structures, i.e. $P(S_1)=P(S_0)=0.5$.

## Prediction for the model comparison

For the model comparison, posterior link probability was mapped to the common judgment scale as a signed structural prediction. For generative tasks, the prediction was $100\,P(S_{1+}\mid D)$; for preventive tasks, it was $-100\,P(S_{1-}\mid D)$. For bidirectional tasks, the hypothesis space contained a no-link structure, $S_0$, a generative-link structure, $S_{1+}$, and a preventive-link structure, $S_{1-}$, with equal prior probabilities. The signed prediction was

$$
\hat y_{\mathrm{link}}
=
100\,P(S_{1+}\mid D)
-
100\,P(S_{1-}\mid D).
$$

Thus, posterior link probability contributed positively for generative evidence, negatively for preventive evidence, and zero for the no-link structure.

## Structure-averaged strength: Estimating causal strength under structure uncertainty {#sec-si-strength}

Structure-averaged strength formalizes the idea that observed data can be informative in two ways: they can indicate how strong a causal relation would be if a link exists, and they can indicate how likely it is that such a link exists at all. A strength estimate that ignores structure uncertainty conditions on $S_1$ and asks how strong $C$ is, assuming that $C$ is a cause of $E$. A structure-averaged estimate instead averages over both possibilities, assigning zero causal strength to the no-link structure and weighting the link-specific strength estimate by the posterior probability of $S_1$. This approach is analogous to other Bayesian model-averaged quantities, such as uncertainty-weighted probability estimates [@Meder2014] or estimates of causal attribution [@stephan2018preemption], but here the quantity of interest is causal strength.

Under structure $S_0$, $C$ and $E$ are independent, and causal strength is fixed to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
w_c^{S_0} &= 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Under $S_1$, causal strength is represented by $w_c$, and is estimated by the posterior expectation

$$
w_c^{S_1}
=
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_1]
=
\int_0^1
w_c\,P(w_c\mid D;S_1)\,dw_c.
$$

<!-- # Equivalently (written in the same style as Meder’s Eq. A6, integrating over the joint posterior) -->

<!-- $$ -->

<!-- \begin{aligned} -->
<!-- w_c^{S_1} -->
<!-- &= \mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D; S_1] \ -->
<!-- &= \iiint w_c\cdot P(\theta\mid D; S_1),d\theta \ -->
<!-- &= \iiint w_c\cdot \frac{P(D\mid \theta; S_1)}{P(D\mid S_1)},P(\theta\mid S_1),d\theta , -->
<!-- \end{aligned} -->
<!-- $$ -->

<!-- where $\theta=(b_c,w_c,w_a)$ under $S_1$ and $w_c$ denotes the $w_c$ component of $\theta$. -->

To obtain a single strength estimate that accounts for uncertainty about whether a causal link exists at all, causal strength is averaged over structures. In the two-structure case, the resulting structure-averaged causal strength is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D]
&=
\sum_{i\in\{0,1\}}
P(S_i\mid D)\,
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_i] \\
&=
P(S_1\mid D)\,w_c^{S_1}
+
P(S_0\mid D)\cdot 0 \\
&=
P(S_1\mid D)\,w_c^{S_1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Put simply, structure-averaged strength equals the estimated causal strength under $S_1$ multiplied by the posterior probability of this causal structure, i.e. the posterior link probability $P(S_1\mid D)$. This estimate reflects both the inferred magnitude of the causal influence under $S_1$ and the posterior probability that a link exists. 

The same model-averaging principle applies to larger hypothesis spaces. For example, if the hypothesis space contains a no-link structure $S_0$, a generative link structure $S_{1+}$, and a preventive link structure $S_{1-}$, the signed structure-averaged estimate is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D]
&=
\sum_{i\in\{0,1+,1-\}}
P(S_i\mid D)\,
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_i] \\
&=
P(S_{1+}\mid D)\,w_c^{S_{1+}}
-
P(S_{1-}\mid D)\,w_c^{S_{1-}}
+
P(S_0\mid D)\cdot 0 \\
&=
P(S_{1+}\mid D)\,w_c^{S_{1+}}
-
P(S_{1-}\mid D)\,w_c^{S_{1-}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the no-link structure contributes zero strength, generative strength contributes positively, and preventive strength contributes negatively. More generally, the same expression applies to any hypothesis space containing multiple candidate causal structures.

## Model implementation

All model and analysis code is available at https://github.com/bmeder/causal_strength_structure_uncertainty. The R code uses Monte Carlo simulation to approximate the integrals by drawing $m = 10^7$ independent samples from the parameter priors. Under $S_1$, each sample consists of $\theta^{(k)}=(b_c^{(k)},w_c^{(k)},w_a^{(k)})$, with all three parameters drawn from independent uniform $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ distributions. Under $S_0$, the free parameters are $b_c$ and $w_a$; $w_c$ is fixed to zero.

The marginal likelihood of each structure is approximated by averaging the likelihood over prior samples:

$$
P(D\mid S_i)
\approx
\frac{1}{m}
\sum_{k=1}^{m}
P(D\mid \theta^{(k)};S_i).
$$
where each $\theta^{(k)}$ is one sample from the parameter prior. Under $S_1$, $\theta^{(k)}=(b_c^{(k)},w_c^{(k)},w_a^{(k)})$, with all three parameters drawn from independent $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ distributions. Under $S_0$, the parameter vector contains only two free parameters, $b_c$ and $w_a$, because $w_c$ is fixed to zero.

The posterior expectation under a fixed structure is computed by likelihood-weighted averaging over the same prior samples. For the link structure $S_1$, the posterior mean causal strength is approximated as

$$
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_1]
\approx
\frac{
\sum_{k=1}^{m}
w_c^{(k)}
P(D\mid\theta^{(k)};S_1)
}{
\sum_{k=1}^{m}
P(D\mid\theta^{(k)};S_1)
}.
$$

Finally, the structure-averaged estimate is computed by weighting the structure-specific estimates by the posterior structure probabilities. Since $w_c=0$ under $S_0$, this reduces to

$$
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D]
=
P(S_1\mid D)\,
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_1).
$$



# Appendix B: Estimating Causal Strength Under Sparse-and-Strong Priors {#sec-appendix-ss}

The Bayesian estimate of causal strength conditional on the link structure depends on the prior distribution assigned to the strength parameters. Whereas the default implementation above uses independent uniform priors, the sparse-and-strong (SS) power model of @Lu2008bayesianpriors assumes systematic prior expectations about the organization of causal systems. Specifically, the SS priors favor explanations in which relatively few causes are effective and effective causes tend to have substantial strength. In the notation used here, $w_a$ denotes the strength of the background cause and $w_c$ the strength of the candidate cause, corresponding to $w_0$ and $w_1$, respectively, in @Lu2008bayesianpriors. We use the SS strength prior defined for inference conditional on the link structure $S_1$, rather than the augmented prior introduced for judgments about causal structure.

## Sparse-and-strong (SS) priors

Under $S_1$, the parameter vector is $\theta=(b_c,w_a,w_c)$, as in @sec-appendix-si. The sparse-and-strong (SS) prior changes the joint prior over the strength parameters $w_a$ and $w_c$, while the prior over the base rate of the candidate cause remains independent and uniform:

$$
b_c \sim \operatorname{Beta}(1,1).
$$

Thus, the full parameter prior under $S_1$ factorizes as

$$
P(\theta\mid S_1)
=
P(b_c)\,
P(w_a,w_c\mid S_1).
$$

The joint prior over $(w_a,w_c)$ differs for generative and preventive relations because the two causal parameterizations imply different roles for the background and candidate causes. 

## Generative relations

For a noisy-OR (generative) relation, the background cause and candidate cause are both potential generators of the effect and therefore compete as alternative causal explanations. The SS prior favors configurations in which one cause is strong and the other is weak. Its density peaks at $(w_a,w_c)=(0,1)$, where the candidate cause is the sole strong cause, and at $(w_a,w_c)=(1,0)$, where the background cause is the sole strong cause.

Following Equation 10 of @Lu2008bayesianpriors, the generative SS prior is given by

$$
P(w_a,w_c\mid S_1, \mathrm{gen})
\propto
e^{-\alpha w_a-\alpha(1-w_c)}
+
e^{-\alpha(1-w_a)-\alpha w_c}.
$$ {#eq-ss-prior-generative}

The parameter $\alpha$ controls how strongly sparse-and-strong causal configurations are preferred. When $\alpha=0$, the prior is uniform over $w_a$ and $w_c$. As $\alpha$ increases, the prior becomes increasingly concentrated around $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$. Following @Lu2008bayesianpriors, we use $\alpha=5$.

## Preventive relations

For a noisy-AND-NOT (preventive) relation, the background cause remains generative, whereas the candidate cause may prevent the effect. Consequently, the background and candidate causes do not compete as alternative generators. Because prevention can be expressed only when the effect would otherwise be generated, the prior favors a strong background cause, $w_a\approx 1$. It has one peak at $(w_a,w_c)=(1,1)$, corresponding to a strong background cause and a strong preventive candidate cause, and another at $(w_a,w_c)=(1,0)$, corresponding to a strong background cause and an ineffective candidate cause.

Following Equation 11 of @Lu2008bayesianpriors, the preventive SS prior is

$$
P(w_a,w_c\mid S_1, \mathrm{prev})
\propto
e^{-\alpha(1-w_a)-\alpha(1-w_c)}
+
e^{-\alpha(1-w_a)-\alpha w_c}.
$$ {#eq-ss-prior-preventive}

As in the generative case, $\alpha=0$ yields a uniform prior, whereas larger values increasingly concentrate prior density around the two favored configurations. We again use $\alpha=5$.

## Posterior causal strength

The SS prior is combined with the appropriate likelihood under $S_1$, using a noisy-OR parameterization for generative relations and a noisy-AND-NOT parameterization for preventive relations. The posterior distribution over the parameters is

$$
P(\theta\mid D;S_1)
=
\frac{
P(D\mid\theta;S_1)\,
P(\theta\mid S_1)
}{
P(D\mid S_1)
}.
$$

The model prediction is the posterior mean of the candidate cause’s strength conditional on $S_1$:

$$
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_1]
=
\int
w_c\,
P(\theta\mid D;S_1)\,
d\theta .
$$ {#eq-ss-posterior-strength}

For a generative relation, $w_c$ represents the probability that the candidate cause generates an effect that would otherwise be absent. For a preventive relation, $w_c$ represents the probability that the candidate cause prevents an effect that would otherwise occur.

## Model implementation

We approximate the posterior expectation by direct Monte Carlo sampling from the SS prior. For each sample $k=1,\ldots,m$, we draw

$$
b_c^{(k)}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)
$$

and draw $(w_a^{(k)},w_c^{(k)})$ from the corresponding generative or preventive SS prior. The two terms in each prior are implemented as an equal-weight mixture of normalized truncated exponential distributions.

For the generative prior, one mixture component concentrates probability near $(w_a,w_c)=(0,1)$ and the other near $(1,0)$. For the preventive prior, one component concentrates probability near $(1,1)$ and the other near $(1,0)$.

Because the parameter samples are drawn directly from the corresponding normalized prior, no additional prior-density weights are required. The posterior mean is approximated by likelihood-weighted averaging:

$$
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_1]
\approx
\frac{
\sum_{k=1}^{m}
w_c^{(k)}
P(D\mid\theta^{(k)};S_1)
}{
\sum_{k=1}^{m}
P(D\mid\theta^{(k)};S_1)
}.
$$

The marginal likelihood under $S_1$ is approximated by

$$
P(D\mid S_1)
\approx
\frac{1}{m}
\sum_{k=1}^{m}
P(D\mid\theta^{(k)};S_1).
$$
# Appendix C: Generating predictions for the model comparison {#sec-appendix-model-comparison}

For the model comparison reported in @sec-human-judgments-reanalysis, each model's predictions were generated using the observed cell frequencies from each experimental condition. Predictions were first computed on the unit interval and then mapped to the common judgment scale.  Model predictions were derived in accordance with the causal framing of the task and mapped to the used response scale. Generative predictions were multiplied by $100$, preventive predictions by $-100$. Bidirectional predictions for conditions in which judgments were given on a $-100$ to $+100$ scale were computed as signed combinations of generative and preventive components.

## Posterior link probability

Posterior link probability was used as the structural prediction, with predictions generated following @griffiths2009theory. For generative and preventive tasks, predictions were the posterior probability of the corresponding link structure relative to the no-link structure. For generative task framing, model prediction were given by

$$
\hat y = 100 \cdot P(S_{1+}\mid D).
$$

For preventive task framing, model prediction were given by

$$
\hat y = -100 \cdot P(S_{1-}\mid D).
$$


For bidirectional tasks, the hypothesis space contained three possible structures: a no-link structure, a generative-link structure, and a preventive-link structure. These structures were assigned equal prior probabilities. Predictions were mapped to the signed response scale by treating posterior probability assigned to a generative link as positive and posterior probability assigned to a preventive link as negative [@griffiths2009theory]: 

$$
\hat y = 100 \cdot P(S_{1+}\mid D) - 100 \cdot P(S_{1-}\mid D).
$$


### Bayesian causal power under sparse-and-strong (SS) priors

For the Bayesian causal-power model with SS priors [@Lu2008bayesianpriors], predictions were the posterior mean causal strength conditional on the generative or preventive link structure $S_1$, depending on task framing. For generative framing, predictions were

$$
\hat y = 100 \cdot \mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_{1+}]
$$

and for preventive framing

$$
\hat y = -100 \cdot \mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_{1-}],
$$

respectively. For bidirectional tasks, following @Lu2008bayesianpriors the posterior mean strengths under the generative and preventive link structures were combined as signed quantities, weighted by their relative marginal likelihoods conditional on a link being present:

$$
\hat y
=
100 \cdot P(S_{1+}\mid D,S_1) \cdot
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_{1+}]
-
100 \cdot P(S_{1-}\mid D,S_1) \cdot
\mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_{1-}],
$$

where

$$
P(S_{1+}\mid D,S_1)
=
\frac{P(D\mid S_{1+})}
{P(D\mid S_{1+})+P(D\mid S_{1-})}
$$

and analogously for $P(S_{1-}\mid D,S_1)$. 

### Structure-averaged causal strength

For structure-averaged strength, predictions incorporated uncertainty about whether a link existed. For generative and preventive tasks, predictions were

$$
\hat y =  100 \cdot P(S_{1+}\mid D) \cdot \mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_{1+}]
$$

and

$$
\hat y = -100 \cdot P(S_{1-}\mid D) \cdot \mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_{1-}],
$$

respectively. For bidirectional tasks, the hypothesis space contained $S_0$, $S_{1+}$, and $S_{1-}$, with equal structure priors. The signed prediction was

$$
\hat y = 100 \cdot P(S_{1+}\mid D) \cdot \mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_{1+}]
-
100 \cdot P(S_{1-}\mid D) \cdot \mathbb{E}[w_c\mid D;S_{1-}]
+
100 \cdot P(S_0\mid D)\cdot 0 .
$$

Thus, generative strength contributed positively, preventive strength negatively, and the no-link structure contributed zero.
